summary:
T -60 Seconds is a co-op web game where 1-4 players learn how real space missions are designed. A disease threatens Earth, and the cure must come from space, so the crew plans and flies three missions: the ISS, the Moon and Mars. Each mission begins with a short educational cutscene.

In the design phase, players take engineering roles and follow the stages NASA uses to mature a mission concept: concept, feasibility, trade studies, point design and a flight readiness review. They vote on objectives and spacecraft, balance shared limits on mass, power and cost, and pack supplies. In the mission phase, they watch space through a capsule window while crises inspired by real NASA incidents, such as solar flares and communication loss, strike. Players must diagnose and repair systems together, while a mission tracker shows progress.

The game addresses the challenge by turning mission design into hands-on trade-offs, not reading. It matters because it teaches teamwork, risk management and engineering decisions to the next generation of space explorers.
details:
What it does

T -60 seconds is a co-op web game where 1-4 players learn how real space missions are designed. A disease threatens Earth and the cure must come from space, so the crew plans and flies three missions: the ISS, the Moon and Mars. Short video cutscenes introduce each destination.

In the design phase, each player takes an engineering role and the team works through the stages NASA uses to mature a mission: concept, feasibility, trade studies, point design and a flight readiness review. Players vote on objectives and spacecraft and balance shared limits on budget, mass and power. They also check life support, communications and redundancy, then pack their resources. In the mission phase, they look out of a capsule window while events based on real NASA missions strike, such as solar flares, communication loss and power shortages. The team must diagnose and fix each one before time runs out. A mission-progress view tracks the flight, and a final debrief explains how their design decisions shaped the outcome.

Benefits and impact

Beginners usually learn mission design as separate theory. Our game lets them feel how mass, power, cost and risk affect each other, and how teamwork decides the result. We want students and space enthusiasts to leave with a simple understanding of systems engineering and an interest in aerospace careers.

Tools

React, TypeScript and Vite for the game, Firebase Realtime Database for game-code rooms and live co-op, and GitHub Pages for hosting. [Add: Three.js for the mission tracker, and any NASA APIs you actually connected.] We used OpenCode and GitHub Copilot as AI coding assistants, and our own review and testing. No special hardware is needed, only a browser.

Creativity

Instead of sliders and menus, the game puts players inside a capsule with a view of space, where warnings appear as risk grows. Roles force real negotiation, and every crisis comes from a real NASA incident.

Factors we considered

Accessibility for beginners (little text, visual feedback), a solo demo mode for single players, accuracy (game units, with NASA sources for real claims), and sound and motion controls.
